summary: Describes mechanisms for transmitting IPv6 packets over Frame Relay networks. It was later updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: Frame Relay is an older way phone companies connect sites. This explains how to send new-style internet messages across it.

how is the link local address formed on frame relay
subtitle: How IPv6 packets are wrapped, addressed and discovered across Frame Relay virtual circuits.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay links are made of separate virtual circuits and have no native multicast, so IPv6 needs rules for framing, address formation and neighbor discovery on them.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets ride in Frame Relay frames marked with NLPID 0x8E, each circuit end point (DLCI) gets its own interface identifier, and Neighbor Discovery messages use two link-layer address formats and are copied onto every circuit to emulate multicast.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from May 1999 and was later updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2590 is a Proposed Standard published in May 1999 and it has been updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Frame Relay Basics
sections.content:
RFC 2590 specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Frame Relay networks, how to form IPv6 link-local addresses on Frame Relay links, and how IPv6 addresses map to Frame Relay addresses. It also defines the content of the Source/Target link-layer address option used in Neighbor Discovery and Inverse Neighbor Discovery messages on such links.

It covers Frame Relay end stations (DTEs) on a public or private network. These end stations can be IPv6 hosts or routers and are called nodes. Nodes are connected by virtual circuits, each identified at an interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI). A DLCI is 10 bits by default, and Frame Relay also defines 16, 17 or 23 bit DLCIs. Circuits can be permanent (PVCs) or switched (SVCs), and the mechanisms apply to both.

Each virtual circuit acts like its own virtual link with its own parameters, distinct from other circuits on the same wire or fiber.
sections.plainLanguage: Offices are joined by private pipes, and each end of a pipe has a number. This paper explains how to send IPv6 messages through those pipes.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
Frame Relay devices are generally configured with a maximum frame size of at least 1600 octets, so the default IPv6 MTU for a Frame Relay interface is 1592. A smaller frame size can be configured, but not smaller than the IPv6 minimum MTU.

A larger MTU can be configured to avoid fragmentation. The limit comes from the CRC used at the HDLC level: CRC16 protects frames up to 4096 bytes, which reduces the effective maximum to approximately 4088 bytes. Configuring an IPv6 MTU above 4080 is strongly discouraged, because IPv6 relies on error detection in the layers above and below it.

For simplicity the specification assumes the same MTU for input and output, even though a circuit may define different sizes for each direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame is like a box with a size limit. The usual box holds 1592 bytes of IPv6 data, and you should not use boxes that are too big or the error check stops working well.

sections.title: The IPv6 Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 encapsulation follows RFC 2427 for both PVCs and SVCs, which lets one circuit carry IPv6 along with other protocols. The NLPID frame format is used, and the IPv6 NLPID value is 0x8E.

A frame holds a Q.922 address of 2 or 4 octets, a Control field of 0x03 (UI), the NLPID 0x8E, the IPv6 packet and the FCS. The Q.922 address carries the DLCI in a 10, 17 or 23 bit form, in canonical bit order.

Protocols that use SNAP encapsulation with their own protocol identifiers are not affected. Their IPv6 identifier must be encoded according to those protocols' specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPv6 message gets a small label on the front saying 'this is IPv6', using the code 0x8E, so the receiver knows what is inside.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
Each circuit end point is treated as a pseudo-interface, so that an autoconfigured IPv6 address, including the link-local address, can be tied to each DLCI. The interface identifier is locally generated and must be unique on the link and on each virtual link terminated on the interface.

It is built from three fields: the EUI bits (the universal/local bit and the individual/group bit, both set to 0), a 38 bit Mid field that adds uniqueness, and a 24 bit DLCI field. A 10, 17 or 23 bit DLCI is extended with zeros to 24 bits. If the DLCI is not known, all 24 bits are set to 1. Duplicate Address Detection is repeated until the identifier, and so the link-local address, is unique.

The Mid field can be made two ways. With local administrative numbers it merges a 6 bit random number, a 16 bit Frame Relay Node Identifier and a 16 bit Frame Relay Link Identifier. Or, if the interface has an E.164 or X.121 number or an NSAP address, that number is truncated to 38 bits, from the high or low order bits.

The link-local address is the prefix FE80::/64 followed by the interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Every pipe end gets its own name tag made of a few parts, including the pipe's number. Then the computer checks nobody else has the same tag.

sections.title: Address Mapping and Link-Layer Address Options
sections.content:
Mapping IPv6 addresses to link-layer addresses uses Neighbor Discovery (ND) and Inverse Neighbor Discovery (IND). The RFC does not define an algorithmic mapping of IPv6 multicast addresses to Frame Relay addresses. It defines two formats for the Source/Target Link-layer Address option.

The DLCI format is used on circuits that exist before the ND or IND exchange, mostly PVCs. The Frame Relay address format is used mostly before an SVC is set up, to learn the remote node's address for an IPv6 address. An implementation may hold both types in its Neighbor Discovery cache.

In both formats the option Type is 1 for a Source and 2 for a Target link-layer address. In the DLCI format the Length is 1 (units of 8 octets), and both low bits of the first address octet are set to 1. In the Frame Relay address format the Length is 2, 3 or 4, depending on the size of the E.164, X.121 or NSAP address, and the first two bits are 0 and 1.
sections.plainLanguage: To find who owns an IPv6 address, computers ask. The answer can be written as a pipe number or as a phone-style number, and this paper says how to write each one.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Frame Relay has no native link-layer multicast, so multicast must be emulated for Neighbor Discovery. A node MUST send frames carrying ND multicast packets to all virtual circuits on the interface. This covers both all-node and solicited-node multicast addresses. A mesh of PVCs dedicated to multicast traffic, or a set of point-to-multipoint PVCs, MAY be used.

On receipt, a Neighbor Discovery Solicitation that carries a Source link-layer address option with a DLCI MUST get Frame Relay specific preprocessing before the ND engine sees it. DLCIs are only locally meaningful, so the sender's DLCI may differ from the receiver's. The receiver stores into the option the DLCI of the circuit on which the frame arrived, as the receiver knows it.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no way to shout to everyone at once, so you whisper the same message down every pipe. When one arrives, the receiver writes its own name for that pipe on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The interface identifier mechanisms provide uniqueness at link (virtual circuit) level. Protection against duplication comes from IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration Duplicate Address Detection. Protection against forgery or accident comes from IPv6 security mechanisms applied to ND or IND messages.

To avoid an IPsec Authentication verification failure, the Frame Relay specific preprocessing of a Solicitation with a DLCI format option MUST be done after the receiver has completed IP Security processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Check the seal on the envelope first, and only then write your own pipe name on it, or the seal will look broken.

fields.name: DLCI
fields.desc: 10, 17 or 23 bit DLCI extended with zeros; all ones if unknown.
